one_liner: C-intrinsics SHA-256/SHA-512 kernels from AWS; only the SHA-NI SHA-256 path beats OpenSSL's assembly, by 5-8%.
what_it_does: Nir Drucker and Shay Gueron (AWS) rewrote OpenSSL-style SHA-256 and SHA-512 compression kernels as C intrinsics (generic, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512 and x86 SHA-NI, plus an ARMv8 SHA-256 extension path) so compiler writers can compare the generated code with hand-written assembly. The public header exposes only one-shot sha256(dgst, data, len, impl) and sha512(...). The caller passes an explicit sha_impl_t, and padding, finalization and the init/update/final steps are static-inline internals, not an exported streaming API. The CMake project builds only a test binary or a speed binary; there is no library target.
how_it_is_fast: The one winning path uses the Intel SHA Extensions (_mm_sha256rnds2_epu32, _mm_sha256msg1/msg2_epu32), following Intel's reference flow with the 64 rounds fully unrolled through unroll pragmas, and clang-9 scheduling it at about 2.80 cycles/byte versus 3.03 for OpenSSL's perlasm SHA-NI. The AVX, AVX2 and AVX-512 paths use Gueron and Krasnov's parallelized message schedule (J Cryptogr Eng 2012), translated from OpenSSL perlasm. The sigma0/sigma1 schedule is vectorized 4 words at a time and computed for 2 blocks (AVX2) or 4 blocks (AVX-512) at once, with W+K stored for the later blocks, while the round function stays scalar. Those paths do not beat OpenSSL.
when_to_use: As a readable reference or vendoring source for a SHA-NI SHA-256 compression function in C (one ~100-line file) when you want to avoid perlasm/.s files in a GCC or Clang build.
Long messages (64 B and up) on x86-64 CPUs with SHA-NI, where the C path measured 1.05x (64 B) to 1.08x (64 KiB) faster than OpenSSL's Feb-2020 SHA-NI assembly on Ice Lake.

Compiler research and codegen regression testing, the authors' stated purpose: compare clang/gcc output for the same algorithm against OpenSSL's hand-scheduled asm, with sanitizer builds and clang-tidy already wired in.
Teaching or porting the Gueron-Krasnov vectorized message-schedule technique to another language or ISA, using intrinsics instead of perl-generated assembly.
when_not_to_use: Production code. The README says it is 'designed to be used for benchmarking purposes only and not in final products'. It ships no library, has had a single commit (2020-05-31), and GitHub issues are disabled.

SHA-512 anywhere, or SHA-256 on CPUs without SHA-NI. Every C AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 path loses to OpenSSL's asm, for example SHA-256 AVX2 709,146 vs 620,729 cycles at 64 KiB (~14% slower) and SHA-512 AVX2 456,221 vs 402,204 (~13% slower). Even the AVX-512 C path (694,132) is slower than OpenSSL's AVX2 asm.
Tiny messages (32 B or less): the SHA-NI C path only ties (281 vs 280 cycles at 32 B, 288 vs 283 at 16 B).
Portable or distributed binaries. Everything is built with -march=native, SIMD support is detected by CMake try_run on the build host, and there is no runtime CPU dispatch.
Many independent messages. Multi-buffer designs such as ISA-L's hash several streams per core, while this code hashes one message at a time.

integration.form: source-drop (CMake project that builds only test/benchmark executables; no static or shared library)
integration.dependencies: OpenSSL libcrypto, linked statically, for the correctness tests and the asm comparison; the copied OpenSSL .s files (x86-64 Linux/macOS, armv8 Linux); CMake 3. The kernels themselves need only compiler intrinsics.
integration.min_toolchain: C99; CMake 3.0+; tested with gcc-9 and clang-9 (the compiler must support AVX2/AVX-512/SHA-NI intrinsics); clang-format-9/clang-tidy-9 for the dev scripts
integration.platforms: x86-64 (generic, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512, SHA-NI for SHA-256 only) and aarch64 (generic, plus an ARMv8 SHA-256 extension C path; SHA-512 generic only); little-endian only; tested on Ubuntu 18.04; macOS x86-64 asm files included; no Windows/MSVC build
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The C paths are reentrant, keeping their context on the stack with no globals. The OPENSSL_* comparison paths set and clear a process-global OPENSSL_ia32cap_P_local/OPENSSL_armcap_P_local around each call, so running them concurrently is a data race.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — produces standard SHA-256/SHA-512 digests, checked against OpenSSL for every length 0-1000 B plus 100,000 Monte Carlo cases, but the API is a one-shot sha256(dgst, data, len, impl) with an explicit implementation enum rather than OpenSSL's SHA256()/EVP interfaces, and there is no streaming update API

gotchas: The sha_impl_t enum members exist only if the build host passed CMake's try_run feature probes, so a binary built on a SHA-NI or AVX-512 machine can SIGILL elsewhere, and choosing a valid implementation is the caller's job.

The AVX2 kernel works on block pairs and routes an odd leftover block through the AVX kernel; the AVX-512 kernel works on 4-block groups. Short inputs therefore run slower on these paths than on plain AVX C (SHA-256 at 1 B: AVX 791, AVX2 821, AVX-512 879 cycles).

Finalization byte-swaps the state on the assumption of a little-endian host. The CMake endianness check uses message(FATAL ...) instead of FATAL_ERROR, so on a big-endian host it probably warns rather than stops.

sha256_update asserts data != NULL before it checks for zero length, so sha256(d, NULL, 0, impl) aborts in builds with asserts enabled, and the entry-point assert uses || and so misses a single NULL pointer. The compress functions also do aligned stores into the state and expect a 64-byte-aligned sha256_state_t if called directly.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over ISA-L Crypto or the S-HASH/j-lanes multi-buffer work only when you need one message's standard SHA-256 digest from auditable C intrinsics rather than assembly; ISA-L is the production choice for many-stream throughput. Over sha256-simd (Go) the choice is simply C versus Go. BLAKE2/BLAKE3 siblings are faster, but only if you can change the hash.
verified_claims_summary: benchmark_example.md was measured on one Dell XPS 13 7390 (Core i7-1065G7 Ice Lake, Turbo off, Ubuntu 18.04.2) with clang-9 at -O3 -march=native. Each cell is the minimum of 10 runs of 100-iteration rdtscp averages after 25 warm-up calls, and the C kernels and the OpenSSL asm (master e32c608e, Feb 24 2020) run through the same sha256() wrapper. Only SHA-256 on SHA-NI wins: 183,685 vs 198,528 cycles at 65,536 B (1.08x, about 2.80 vs 3.03 cycles/byte) and 424 vs 446 at 64 B (1.05x), tied at 32 B or less. Every AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 C path and all of SHA-512 lose to OpenSSL.
status_note: Abandoned: a single initial commit on 2020-05-31, issues disabled, 21 stars, and never re-measured against OpenSSL 3.x. It is Apache-2.0, and the SHA-NI kernel is small enough to vendor; the last known-good compilers are gcc-9/clang-9.
